title: Inertial Asynchronous Computation
authors: Doruk Efe Gökmen, Michel Fruchart, Dmitrii Zendrikov, Giacomo Indiveri, Giulio Biroli, Vincenzo Vitelli
abstract: Computation is the controlled evolution of a state. Asynchronous evolutions, where all parts of the state change in their own time without stopping each other, put this control in jeopardy. It is in fact a mystery how natural processes perform asynchronous computations using many units with no global orchestration. Here we demonstrate how collective computational abilities can emerge in asynchronous many-body systems. The key insight is to split the physical "hardware" underlying the computation into two asymmetrically coupled parts, analogous to position and momentum in a harmonic oscillator. The resulting inertia nudges the evolution of the state so that the asynchronous computation proceeds in the right order. By treating our inertial asynchronous computer as a nonequilibrium material, we map out its phase diagram numerically and analytically using a framework we dub loop dynamical mean-field theory. We experimentally demonstrate our approach using analog spiking neuromorphic chips designed to mimic actual neurons in the brain. In addition, we construct software that can run on asynchronous hardware: we denoise movies whose clean versions were never seen during training, an instantiation of the generalization transition underlying modern machine learning. Our results point to a general strategy for reliable, decentralized computation in energy-constrained settings from dynamics self-assembly to cell differentiation.
summary: This work proposes that reliable computation in decentralized, asynchronous physical systems requires an inertial mechanism. By modeling the system using coupled position and momentum variables, the authors demonstrate how this inertia guides the state evolution to correctly retrieve temporal sequences. The findings are supported by theoretical phase diagram analysis and experimental implementation on neuromorphic hardware.
main_problem: The core problem is understanding how natural processes can perform reliable, ordered computation when components update asynchronously without a global clock.
main_result: Inertia, modeled by coupling position and momentum variables, provides the necessary mechanism to guide asynchronous state evolution toward correct computational sequences.
method: The authors employ loop dynamical mean-field theory to analyze the phase diagram of the system, supplemented by experimental validation on neuromorphic chips.
model_or_system: The model is an inertial asynchronous computation network where physical hardware is split into two asymmetrically coupled parts (position $\mathbf{x}$ and momentum $\mathbf{p}$). The dynamics are governed by coupled, non-variational update rules.
key_observables: Order parameters ($m_\mu(t)$ for static retrieval; $m_d$ for sequence retrieval), phase diagram boundaries (Blackout, Static Retrieval, Sequence Retrieval).
important_parameters: The ratio of patterns to neurons ($P/N$), the inertial coupling strength ($\lambda$), and the memory load.
main_assumptions: The approach assumes that coupling position and momentum in this specific manner provides a general strategy for reliable, decentralized computation.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the concept of inertia enabling successful asynchronous computation compared to failure modes. Later panels show concrete results contrasting synchronous success, asynchronous failure, and proposed model success in associative memory retrieval.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the mystery of natural asynchronous computation, proposes the inertial $\mathbf{x}/\mathbf{p}$ model, develops the theoretical framework using loop DMFT to map the phase diagram, and concludes with experimental demonstrations on neuromorphic hardware and software applications like movie denoising.
why_interesting: The concept of emergent order from local, asynchronous interactions, mediated by an 'inertial' memory term, provides a rich analogy for understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in open quantum systems or complex many-body physics where global control is absent.

The phase diagram obtained from Monte-Carlo simulations (C; see Methods for details) shows three behaviors, that we interpret as thermodynamic phases in the limit where both the number N of neurons and the number of stored patterns P go to infinity, at fixed memory load P/N.
